newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraqi oil exports leave Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi oil exports leave Gulf.

text.p: A supertanker laden with Iraqi crude has left an Iraqi port for the first time in six years, Gulf oil industry sources said on Wednesday.
The 274,000 deadweight tonnes tanker Star Africa departed from the Mina al-Bakr export terminal under a United Nations oil-for-food deal late on Tuesday.
"It left last night...It should be out of the Gulf in the next 30 hours," a Gulf shipping source briefed with day-to-day operations at the terminal said.
A second tanker, the Leonidas, has completed loading Iraqi crude and is expected to leave al-Bakr as soon as documentation for the cargo is cleared, the source added.

Under the U.N. deal Iraq is allowed to export $2 billion of its oil over six months to pay for much-needed humanitarian supplies after six years of crippling international sanctions following its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Under the strictly monitored deal, Iraq is allowed to export only from the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan and al-Bakr through U.N.-approved contracts.
The first cargo under the deal, which is expected to see some 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraq oil reaching the international markets, left Ceyhan on Monday. That cargo will stay in Turkey.

The Star Africa has been chartered by U.S. energy firm Coastal Corp under a six-month 60,000 bpd contract and traders said the Texas-based firm would take the ship to its refinery on the Caribbean island of Aruba.

For Coastal, the departure of the tanker represents the resumption of multi-million dollar commercial ties with Baghdad which were cut when the U.N. slapped sanctions on the export of Iraqi crude after the 1990-91 Gulf Crisis.

In December 1990, just prior to the Gulf War, Coastal's flamboyant owner Oscar Wyatt met Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and other senior Iraqi officials to secure the release of 32 American hostages who were then flown back to the United States in a Coastal-chartered jet.

Wyatt has been critical of the duration of the sanctions. He and other Coastal executives have frequently attended ministerial conferences of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) held in Europe.
Before August 1990, Coastal accounted for some 10 percent of Iraq's total crude sales.
"Coastal have always remained close to the Iraqis...Its refinery in Aruba is set up to run off their crude," one Western oil executive based in the Gulf said.

For Iraq the exports from Turkey and the Gulf represent a crucial return to the international market and a chance to recapture customers lost to other producers -- including those in the Middle East -- over the last six years.
The first oil tanker to take Iraqi crude to Japan will load at al-Bakr on January 24, shipping brokers said.
But Baghdad will still be far away from its pre-war exports of 2.7 million bpd which earned it $18 billion a year.
